title: Capacity Backstop Scaling Ladder — Oct 2025
content:
Purpose:
This sheet defines a pragmatic scaling ladder (backstop tiers) for GPU capacity across regions to cover staggered failures, abrupt demand surges, and planned maintenance windows. The ladder is intended to minimize customer-visible impact while keeping cost and idle capacity within predictable bounds.

Summary Ladder (activation order):
- Level 0 (Normal): baseline pools + dynamic autoscale (utilization target 70-80%).
- Level 1 (Buffer): activate per-region warm buffer pools (sized as baseline * buffer_pct). Cold-start allowed <30s for non-latency-critical routes.
- Level 2 (Backstop): spin up cross-region backstop pools (preemptible where acceptable, or dedicated reserved for enterprise customers). Route selective traffic by model tier.
- Level 3 (Emergency): full cross-region failover + degraded SLOs (token rate limits, shorter context windows, fallbacks to smaller model family).

Assumptions (simulation inputs):
- Traffic distribution: us-west1 45%, us-east1 25%, europe-west 20%, asia-southeast 10%.
- Typical sustained token throughput per GPU (A100-80GB): 2.8M tokens/day under target batching profile.
- Acceptable latency degradation windows: 2–5 minutes for Level 1; 10–30 minutes for Level 2 activation; Level 3 immediate protective throttling.
- Cost assumptions: warm buffer GPU: 30% of reserved price (via spot + fast-attach), backstop reserved GPU: 100% reserved price.

Region-by-region baseline and ladder (example numbers):
Columns: Region | GPU Type | Baseline GPUs | Buffer % | Buffer GPUs | Backstop GPUs | Level-3 Failover Target | Notes
us-west1 | A100-80GB | 240 | 12% | 29 | 60 | absorb 60 GPUs from eu / on-demand burst | primary traffic zone, largest buffer
ue-east1 | A100-80GB | 120 | 15% | 18 | 30 | shift to us-west1 and europe | second-tier critical region
europe-west | A100-80GB | 160 | 10% | 16 | 40 | accept reduced model size until recovery | enterprise customers routed to reserved backstop
asia-southeast | A100-80GB | 80 | 20% | 16 | 24 | prioritize latency-sensitive shards to local warm pool | smaller baseline requires proportionally larger buffer

Scaling ladder activation criteria (metric-based):
- Queue latency (95p) exceeds 450ms for >1m -> Level 1 warm buffer activation for affected region.
- Error rate (5xx) or GPU preemption events >0.8% in 10m -> Level 2 cross-region backstop spin-up for same model family.
- Cloud region outage (console status) or sustained >80% of baseline GPUs offline -> Level 3 emergency failover.

Routing & gradation rules:
- Prefer intra-region buffer first (Level 1). If Level 1 fully allocated and SLOs still missed, route 20% of new requests to backstop models (smaller model variants) while warming additional backstop GPUs.
- Backstop capacity should be compatible with model family; use quantized variants if available to increase capacity per GPU.
- During Level 3, enforce token-rate caps per token-second budget for free-tier/low-tier customers; enterprise customers routed to reserved pools where possible.

Operational playbook (short checklist):
1) Trigger detection: automated alerts via metrics alerting (Prometheus -> PagerDuty).
2) Owner initial action (SRE on-call): verify region health, check K8s node conditions, GPU preemption logs.
3) Level 1: run 'warm-pool-attach' job; validate model kernel warm start; update routing rules in Envoy.
4) Level 2: allocate backstop ASG, attach GPUs, run health-check and KV cache prefetch for top-tier prompts; enable partial traffic split (10-30%).
5) Level 3: enact cross-region failover playbook; engage on-call infra lead and product comms; enable degraded-mode experience flags.

Test & validation plan (quarterly):
- Tabletop exercises: simulate 1-region full outage; measure time to Level 2 and Level 3 milestones.
- Chaos tests: preempt 15% of GPUs in us-west1 during peak window and validate that routing keeps p95 latency < target when ladder is used.
- Cost burn test: estimate monthly cost of maintaining Level 1 buffers always-on vs on-demand attach behavior.

Sizing rationale and cost snapshot (monthly incremental cost estimate):
- Keep Level 1 warm buffers as lightweight warm-attached instances (fast attach) to keep always-on cost ~10–15% of baseline. Example: us-west1 buffer 29 GPUs -> incremental $~65k/month (fast-attach pricing).
- Backstop reserved (Level 2) held as shared reserved pools in two regions to reduce cold-start latency; cost depends on reservation contracts. Example backstop pool total 154 GPUs -> approximate $~320k/month if fully reserved (sensitivity +/− 20%).

Open questions & decisions needed:
- Acceptable spot/preemptible mix for backstop pools for non-enterprise traffic? (tradeoff: cost vs reliability)
- How aggressively do we throttle free-tier users during Level 3? (policy and product alignment)
- Should Level 1 buffers be regional RUs (warm-attach) or local VM snapshot + hibernation strategy?

Immediate action items (owner: Samira Patel):
- [ ] Run a dry-run tabletop for us-west1 outage with on-call SRE and product ops (target date: 2025-11-10).
- [ ] Create JIRA tasks to provision a 60-GPU cross-region reserved backstop pool (JIRA-INF-7641).
- [ ] Draft customer-facing incident template for degraded inference experience (owner: Priya Desai).

Appendix: quick command snippets for responders
- Attach warm pool (internal tool): infractl pools attach --region us-west1 --count 30 --pool warm-backstop
- Promote backstop to primary routing: infractl routing promote --from europe-west --to us-west1 --percent 25

Notes on uniqueness: this sheet focuses on a \"ladder\" metaphor (levels with gradated actions and cost tradeoffs) and includes concrete metric triggers, per-region sample numbers, and a short test plan oriented toward quarterly rehearsals. Intentionally avoids large heatmaps or pure allocation matrices — it's a tactical playbook that sits between a checklist and a sizing worksheet.
